display_title: Official Review of Paper4022 by Reviewer Jubu

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Caro, a framework for detecting Out-of-domain (OOD) utterances within dialogues. The authors claim that they are one of the first to create an OOD method incorporating the full dialogue history as opposed to using only a single turn, while also addressing the problem of long-range dependencies between turns.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I first summarize the strengths and weaknesses and later provide actionable feedback.

# Summary of Strengths:
- Comparison with other models hints at the superiority of Caro.
- Ablation experiments empirically demonstrate some strengths of the proposed method

# Summary of Weaknesses:
- The description of the methodology is not easy to follow. After reading the explanations several times I still have too many questions regarding how everything fits together.
- Mathematical notation hinders the exposition instead of supporting it.
- Too many claims are not empirically supported

# Suggestions and questions for the authors

- The abstract emphatically states that "previous OOD intent detection approaches are limited to single-turn contexts", which can be easily construed as you being the first to incorporate the full context, which we know is not true. Later in the introduction you tone this statement down by mentioning that "most OOD intent detection approaches are limited to single turn inputs". To be fair to previous efforts and less misleading I suggest accompanying this statement with references to previous work both incorporating single-turn and multi-turn contexts.

- Contribution 3 in the Introduction states that you conduct extensive experiments in two benchmark datasets. I would first counter this claim by saying that the STAR dataset is just a Task-oriented Dialogue dataset, not a benchmark dataset. I think that the word "benchmark" in the field of NLP invokes thoughts of a collection of tasks (for example the GLUE or SuperGLUE benchmarks), and could be interpreted as something much harder than it is actually being achieved in the paper. Second, you mention that there were two benchmark datasets, while in reality it is only the STAR dataset which you downsampled. So I suggest removing the word "benchmark" and saying that you test your method in different "splits" or versions of the same dataset.

- You mention that your approach helps tackle the "long distance obstacle" which I assume means the same as the difficulty in modeling long-term dependencies in Language. I understand that the multi-view approach based on the bottleneck method is supposed to incorporate inductive biases that should alleviate this issue by removing superfluous information passed from turn to turn, however there are no experiments for verifying that this is actually true. The ablation on the representation learning loss provides directional evidence by showing that methods that do not use this bottleneck-based method perform worse. However to strengthen your case I would further show how different methods perform in contexts of varying lengths. Showing that your method consistently performs better in turns with longer contexts would definitely provide more evidence supporting this claim.

- Math notation could be greatly improved.
  - In section 2 you define $\mathcal{D}_I$ as $\lbrace(x_i, y_i)\rbrace$ which literally means a set containing a single tuple $(x_i, y_i)$. You correctly defined $\mathcal{I}$ as the set of $I_i$ for $i=1$ to $k$. I suggest being consistent when defining $\mathcal{D}_I$, and specifying the $i$ indices going from $i=1$ to $|\mathcal{D}_i|$ for example. Similarly you define $\mathcal{D}_U$ as $\tilde{x_i}$, which means a set containing the single $\tilde{x_i}$ element.

  - Further, you mention that $\mathcal{D}_U$ is a set of unlabeled samples $\tilde{x_i}$, but immediately after you say that the label of $\tilde{x_i}$ is in $\mathcal{I} \cup I_\{k+1\}$ so $\tilde{x_i}$ does have a label. Similarly in 4.2 you say that you leveraged the labels from $\mathcal{D}_U$. I think that to simplify your notation you can avoid explicitly defining the test set $\mathcal{D}_T$. You can say that  $\mathcal{D}_I$ is the set of $(x, y)$ tuples for the known intents (with labels referencing $\mathcal{I}$), and $\mathcal{D}_U$ is the set of $(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y})$ tuples for all the intents (including the OOD intent $I_\{k-1\}$). Then you can specify that your test data is a subset of $\mathcal{D}_U$ and that during training the model is not shown the $\tilde{y}$ labels.

  - Additionally you type both $\mathcal{I} \cup I_{k+1}$ and $\mathcal{I} \cup \lbrace I_{k+1}\rbrace$. To be technically correct you should use only the latter.

  - Later you say that $z^j \sim e(z^j|v^j)$, where $e(z^j|v^j)$ is an encoder. Saying that a random variable follows an "encoder" distribution is too big an abuse of notation. I suggest rewriting this to properly distinguish theory from practice, i.e. $z^j$ follows a distribution which is parametrized by an encoder.

  - You then mention that Eq. 1 "ensures that the representation $z^1$ for $v^1$ is sufficient for $v^2$". I suggest clarifying what you mean by a representation being "sufficient" in this context.

  - Later you mention that your feature extractor $f$ is implemented as a BERT model. But then I get confused because your BERT encoder is not $e(z^j|v^j)$ which you mentioned was an encoder. I am guessing that $e(z^j|v^j)$ is actually implemented as the MLP which receives as input the features returned by the BERT model, correct? If that is the case I suggest clarifying it in the text.

  - I suggest not assuming that readers will be familiar with non-mainstream approaches. In the description of the first stage of the multi-stage training approach you reference the approach by Zhang et al. 2021 without giving any details about it. It would greatly help your exposition if you at least summarized what the approach is.

  - In stage two you reference $\mathcal{D}_{PL}$ without having defined it. I suggest defining it before referencing it.

  - In the third stage you mention a classifier $p$ on top of the already defined models $e$ and $f$. Is the classifier $p$ equivalent to the encoder $e$ that you defined previously? Is it only the MLP that you define later? I suggest making this clear in the text.

- After reading several times, it is still not clear to me how the $\mathcal{C}(x)$ set is built. In 3.2 you mention that for each x in $\mathcal{D}_I$ you retrieve $M$ samples from $\mathcal{D}_U$ that share similar contexts with $x$. But nothing else is mentioned in this section about how $\mathcal{C}(x)$ is produced, or how context similarity is measured. In the third stage description you say that you use the classifier $p$ trained with the pseudo-labels in stages one and two to filter out the candidates in $\mathcal{C}(x)$ that have high IND confidence scores, but how high? What threshold did you use? Also, I think it would be a good idea to do a calibration analysis of the resulting $p$ classifier after stages one and two, and report Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) if you are relying on a classifier's confidence scores. Finally, these context scores are not necessarily equivalent context similarity. You could argue that it is a proxy fur such, but then you have to better explain why you think so.

- In eq. 3 the symbol $CE$ is not defined. It will not be obvious to every reader that it means Cross Entropy. Also, according to figure 1, $v = f(x)$, but in eq. 3 you use $p(f(x))$ in the first sum and $p(v)$ in the second. Again, the exposition would be more clear if used consistent symbols: either $f(x)$ or $v$ in both sums.

- In the final paragraph of page 4 you make three claims, all of which are unsupported to that point of the paper. So I suggest putting these claims, and any discussion in general, after the experiments and results. However, even when taking the experiments and results into account, the two of the three claims do not hold their ground (the first and third).

  - "Learning robust representations makes IND and OOD  samples more separable and helps synthesize high quality representations for pseudo OOD labels": What does it mean for a representation to be robust? how did you prove that they are more separable and help synthesize high quality representations for pseudo OOD labels? I could not make the connection between the experiment results and this claim.

  - "An effective and evolving classifier helps to more effectively filter out IND samples from the candidate pool": Since the filtering procedure is not clear and the classifier was not explicitly calibrated, I am not convinced that this claim is true. It would also be worth to explain what you mean with an "evolving" classifier.

- At the end of paragraph 2 in sec. 4.3 you mention that InfoMax achieves the lowest performance compared to other models and then jumped to the conclusion that this means that eliminating superfluous information is important. First it was not proven that Caro effectively eliminates superfluous information. Second, just performing better than a model that does not allegedly remove superfluous information in a single dataset is not sufficient for concluding that the better model does, nor does that mean that the elimination of superfluous information is the cause for better performance.

- Finally, references to the Bottleneck Principle are sprinkled throughout the paper, but I could not understand what the link of your contribution was to it. The main explanation mentions that its main property is that it discards superfluous information producing more robust features (page 3, paragraph 2), but as mentioned above, it was never proven that the final approach does indeed remove superfluous information, so I missed the point of putting so much emphasis on this principle.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall the clarity of the paper is low, and there is no statement mentioning the intention of making the code and experiments public, so I judge reproducibility to be also low.

I consider the novelty of the paper to be minimal, considering that the claims that constitute the essence of the paper are not well founded. See details in "Suggestions and questions for the authors"
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is unclear and does not provide sufficient evidence to support its fundamental claims, which is why I am inclined to reject it.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a context-aware OOD intent detection (Caro) framework for out-of-domain (OOD) intent detection. Specifically, this work is motivated to address two problems in this field. First, the proposed model utilizes an unsupervised representation learning loss to learn robust representations that are most related to the intent detection task given a long and noisy dialogue. Second, pseudo OOD samples are synthesized with the help of unlabeled data under the constraint of dialogue contexts. Those contents are more likely to be seen in practice. The authors use a three-stage training strategy to filter the in-domain samples when constructing pseudo OOD samples. Experiments and analyses on STAR dataset verify the effectiveness of their method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
	
1. The setting of history-dependent intent detection is interesting.

2. The idea of constructing OOD samples under the constraint of dialogue contexts makes sense and is practical in real-life scenario.

Weaknesses:

1. About the choice of datasets. The experiments are only conducted in one dataset. Although the authors claim that STAR is a dataset that is designed to be strongly history-dependent, it is better to test Caro in datasets that are most widely-used by previous works like CLINC150, StackOverflow and Banking, etc., under the history-aware setting. 

On one hand, the superiority of Caro over previous history-independent models should be demonstrated in this more convincing way since those datasets already contain some recognized results. 

On the other hand, only by Caro still obtaining performance gains on these datasets that are not as history-dependent as STAR, can the claim of “since multi-turn contexts are generally critical for practical intent detection tasks” be convincingly recognized.

2. About the selection of backbone model. The authors test Caro with bert-base-uncased, which is a relatively weak pre-trained language model. The conclusion could be more convincing if the authors test their model on some stronger PLMs like the large version of ELECTRA or Deberta since the performance gains may become minor under those powerful PLMs (especially the effect of L_UR may become minor).

Questions:

1. What if λ is set to 0? This ablation is vital but is not presented in the paper.

2. What are the differences between the “Pseudo-label” in Table 2 and FM in table 4? The former is way better and why don’t you use it in the first training stage?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and the claims are generally clarified. The technique is somewhat novel in the scope of  OOD intent detection.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the OOD problem discussed in this paper is interesting and the solution is sound. The experimental part is relatively weak. Only one dataset is used for evaluations. The baseline model is relatively weak, too.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper has proposed a new method for OOD detection for multi-turn task-oriented dialogues. The new method involves two aspects: one is robust representation learning, and the other is the data augmentation/synthesizing with data filtering.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The proposed robust representation learning looks beneficial.
2. The proposed data augmentation method with data selection can bring in improvement.

Weakness:
1. The proposed two techniques are actually able to generalize to any kinds of OOD detection, which should not be constraint to multi-turn dialogues. This paper claims to focus on multi-turn dialogues OOD detection, but the methods are not specific to the multi-turn setting.
2. Some parts of methods are not clear and missing information there and I will post some questions on these part in the next section.
3. I think there are some baselines that are missing:
   (1) Revisiting Mahalanobis Distance for Transformer-Based Out-of-Domain Detection
   (2) Discriminative Nearest Neighbor Few-Shot Intent Detection by Transferring Natural Language Inference
   (3) One baseline is that for multi-turn dialogues, how about we first rewrite the last utterance to resolve the missing information by using the context, e.g. anaphors and ellipsis. Then we use those best OOD methods on the rewritten utterances by treating it as a single-turn OOD detection problem? I think this is the key to showing the difference of multi-turn and single-turn OOD detection. 
4. The comparison in Table 2 is unfair. All baselines can only use D_I data while the method proposed can use both D_I+D_U data. 
5. I have concerns on the proposed robust representation learning method, which is outlined in the next section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Here are my questions on the method section for clarity:
1. In section 3.1, what is the encoder? How is it implemented? 
2. What is so-called superfluous information?
3. In section 3.2, how do you obtain samples that have similar contexts?
4. In section 3.3, please elaborate the method from Zhan et al. 2021 for stage 1.
5. What is the typical size of C(x) in equation 2?

I have several questions on the robust representation learning method:
1. I actually quite understand the intuition behind this method. It proposes first obtaining the two dropout representations using the same BERT encoder and then try to minimize the distance between the two representations after sampling from a Gaussian distribution. Why does it help to make the model more robust? Why does it help improve OOD detection?
2. How does this method compare with some other representation learning methods, such as MLM, or SimCSE (SimCSE: Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings)?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper looks quite ok in my first look but after second thought, I think there are many aspects that need to be improved or clarified, which have been described in details above.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this work, the authors tackle the problem of OOD intent detection for dialogue systems. To tackle this problem, the authors introduce a new framework called Context aware OOD intent detection (Caro) that performs OOD intent detection using multi-turn contexts.


Contributions:
1. New framework Caro to build OOD intent detection for dialogue systems and unlike previous approaches Caro using multi-turn contexts for OOD intent detection.
2. Caro learns robust representation for intent detection through the use of multi-view information bottleneck principle.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths and Weakness:
1. The authors tackle an interesting problem of OOD intent detection for dialog systems through the introduction of a novel framework Caro for multi-turn dialog contexts.
2. More information is needed about robust representation learning section: How is the input space optimized when the x = <h,u> is provided as input to the model? This framework is optimized for multi-turn contexts, how are extremely long contexts provided as input?
3. Results on the STAR-full and small benchmark datasets show that the proposed approach using Caro outperforms existing baselines and other state of the art approaches for the similar task.
4. One thing that is missing from the paper that would add value is the lack of error analysis in terms of the type of mistakes this approach makes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The Caro framework is novel and tackles the problem of OOD detection. The authors do a good job of evaluation and compare multiple baseline and state of the art approaches on the same dataset to evaluate the performance.
content.summary_of_the_review: In this work, the authors tackle the problem of OOD intent detection for dialogue systems by introducing a new framework called Context aware OOD intent detection (Caro) that performs OOD intent detection using multi-turn contexts. Results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
